🎓 How a CMU PhD Student Takes a Paper From 0 to 1
After three semesters as a PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, Zhihu contributor 郑深 shared the workflow he uses to turn an early research idea into a conference submission.
His first year included funding uncertainty, an ICCV 2025 acceptance for ROADWork and a Waymo internship. He is now preparing or submitting two first-author papers.
His main lesson is that research rarely starts with a perfect idea. It advances through reproducibility, failure analysis and disciplined iteration.

1️⃣ Start with a tractable research problem
For junior PhD students, the most efficient starting point is usually talking to advisors and senior students about available projects.
The ideal direction has high potential but limited competition. If that opportunity is unavailable, look for a concrete weakness in existing work.
Begin with recent surveys from the past one or two years. Then select around ten representative top-conference papers with strong results, high citations and open-source code.
At first, focus on titles, abstracts, figures and tables. In fast-moving areas such as text-to-image generation, papers older than one year may already be less relevant.

2️⃣ Choose datasets and metrics conservatively
Prefer public datasets that the community already uses. They make comparisons easier and reduce unexpected engineering costs.
Before modifying or building a dataset, estimate:
· Compute requirements
· Annotation cost
· Engineering workload
· Delivery time
Apply the same discipline to evaluation metrics. If an existing metric ignores important objects, rare events or safety-critical cases, improving it may become part of the research contribution.
Otherwise, keep the standard metric. Changing datasets and metrics too early creates unnecessary variables.

3️⃣ Reproduce a strong baseline before proposing anything
Choose one representative, high-quality paper as the baseline.
First, run its released pretrained checkpoint. Then train the model yourself and verify that you can reproduce the reported result.
If the baseline cannot be reproduced after reasonable effort, reconsider it. Building a new method on top of an unstable baseline makes every later conclusion difficult to trust.
Only after reproduction should you read the method and implementation in detail.

4️⃣ Let failure cases reveal the research question
Visualize the baseline’s outputs and combine qualitative observations with quantitative metrics.
Group failures into clear categories:
· Small objects
· Occlusion
· Rare scenarios
· Missing context
· Incorrect associations
· Unstable predictions
This turns “the model is not good enough” into a set of testable problems.
The next step is recursive ablation. Remove or replace one module, retrain the system and measure what changes. Continue decomposing the components with the largest impact.
This process reveals both how the model works and where a meaningful contribution may exist.

🔍 Two outcomes lead to different research strategies
If removing modules consistently reduces performance, the existing architecture is probably well designed.
You may need a genuinely new modeling idea. This is difficult to solve through intuition alone, so discussions with advisors and senior researchers become especially valuable.
If removing a component improves performance, the opportunity is more direct.
Study related alternatives, replace the problematic component and treat the improved system as a new baseline. Then continue iterating until your own module emerges from the process.
A good research idea is often discovered through controlled removal, not added complexity.

5️⃣ Implement the smallest possible version first
Once you have an idea, test it with the least code and time possible.
Do not begin by tuning hyperparameters.
🔹 Write an independent Python script to verify that the new module is feasible.
🔹 Integrate it into the existing repository and make inference work before training.
🔹 Start with a small training subset, but always evaluate on the full test set.
A failed minimal experiment is cheap. A failed experiment buried inside a large codebase can consume days before revealing that the original idea was flawed.

6️⃣ Treat experiment management as part of research
Clean engineering makes conclusions easier to trust.
Use one base configuration, such as exp_base.yaml, and keep each experimental config limited to a small number of changes.
Give experiments traceable names. Commit and push after every successful small modification.
Use separate Git branches for larger architectural changes. Merge them only after confirming compatibility with the main pipeline.
This prevents a common research failure: obtaining a good result but being unable to identify which code, configuration or checkpoint produced it.

7️⃣ Scale experiments in stages
Train on a subset first to check whether the idea moves the metric in the expected direction. Once the pipeline is stable, run the complete training set.
Evaluation should remain on the full test set throughout the process.
Repeat implementation and validation until:
· The method clearly outperforms existing approaches
· The improvement is consistent
· Further gains cannot be explained by simple tuning
· Failure cases have changed in the expected direction
Then expand the evaluation to additional datasets and metrics.

8️⃣ Write figures before prose
When the experiments are complete, start the paper with figures and tables.
Next, build the argument around them:
1. What problem does the baseline have?
2. Why does the proposed method address it?
3. Which experiments support that claim?
4. Where does the method still fail?
Only then fill in the prose.
Starting with visual evidence makes it harder for the paper to drift into claims unsupported by the experiments.

🧘 Avoiding burnout is part of the workflow
Research productivity depends on sustained attention, not occasional all-nighters.
The author recommends reducing short-video and social-media use, sleeping enough and finding reliable ways to recover through food, music, exercise or a spa.
When progress feels difficult, talk to other people instead of remaining isolated. Senior students can also serve as realistic examples of how research careers develop.
Rest is not time taken away from research. Clear thinking and creative work depend on it.

🔑 The complete 0-to-1 loop
The workflow can be summarized as:
Choose a tractable problem → reproduce a baseline → classify its failures → ablate its modules → test the smallest new idea → scale carefully → write around evidence.
The critical step is not brainstorming a complicated architecture.
It is building a process that repeatedly converts observations into falsifiable experiments.

4 stages of LLM training, clearly explained:

(a popular LLM interview question; bookmark this)

→ Pre-training
→ Instruction fine-tuning
→ Preference fine-tuning
→ Reasoning fine-tuning

The visual covers all of them.

A base model treats a question as text to be continued, not a request to be answered. Questions in its training data usually have more questions next to them, so that's what the model replies.

The stages after pre-training allow changing that behaviour, and each one uses a different training signal to do it.

0) Randomly initialized model

The weights are random numbers, so token selection is close to uniform, and the LLM outputs gibberish text.

1) Pre-training

The model reads a large text corpus and repeatedly predicts the next word.

This stage teaches the model grammar and facts about the world.

Also, most of its raw reasoning ability comes from this stage, and it's where nearly all of the training compute goes.

The model becomes good at continuing text, but nothing in the objective connects a question to an answer.

2) Instruction fine-tuning

Here, it trains on pairs of instructions and good responses, so it picks up the convention that a question should get an answer and a request to summarise should get a summary.

OpenAI used roughly 13,000 human-written examples on GPT-3, against a pre-training corpus of hundreds of billions of words.

The knowledge was already in the weights, and this stage mostly taught a response format.

3) Preference fine-tuning

A lot of requests have no single correct answer, and supervised fine-tuning needs a specific target to train against.

In this setup, two responses go to a human who picks the better one. You may have already seen this in ChatGPT, where it asks which of the two responses is better.

Those picks train a separate model that predicts which response a human would have chosen. The main model then gets updated to score higher against that predictor.

4) Reasoning fine-tuning

For maths and code, there's usually one correct answer, and a program can check it. Human preference isn't needed here, since correctness is already a usable reward signal.

The model attempts a problem, the answer gets checked, and it's rewarded when it gets it right.

DeepSeek trained R1 this way with GRPO, and behaviours like working through intermediate steps and going back to fix its own mistakes showed up during training without any examples demonstrating them.

That said, stage 4 only works when a program can check the answer. Maths and code inherently provide that.

But a support reply, a RAG answer, or a summary has no correct output to check against, so the reward has to come from somewhere else.

I wrote a full breakdown of how labs are handling that problem, from RLHF through GRPO, and what replaced the checker.

A 21-YEAR-OLD CHINESE GIRL MAKES $12,000+ A MONTH WITH A DANCING ANIME GIRL THAT DOESN’T EVEN EXIST

No, I’m not talking about game development or animation.

She simply dances in front of a camera.

AI turns every movement, facial expression, and gesture into a realistic anime avatar that copies her perfectly.

That’s the version she posts online. Not herself.

Millions of people follow the character. Most of them don’t even care who’s controlling it.

Fashion brands pay the avatar to wear their clothes. Beauty companies pay the avatar to promote their products. Gaming studios pay the avatar to appear in campaigns.

The audience never bought into the AI. They bought into the personality.

That’s the biggest misconception about AI creators.

People don’t follow technology. They follow characters they enjoy watching.

The creators who understand that first will build the next generation of internet celebrities.
